Design gallery

Failure and recovery: five traps and the ways back

What an analyst sees when graphty gives a wrong-looking answer, a right-looking wrong answer, or no answer at all, and how they get back. Five branches on real data, each tagged with its kind of failure.

How to read the frames. Each picture is the part of a live screen mock that matters, at a readable size, with the region the frame turns on outlined in dashes and a small whole-screen locator beside it; the full screen, with light and dark and an annotation layer, is one click away. Lines marked "Expected reaction" are the design's hypothesis in the persona's voice, not something a person said. Each branch ends with the bet the study tests, what passes, and the miss path.

The three people

  • Alex, an operations analyst (persona), is trying graphty on the Les Miserables sample (77 characters, 254 co-appearances) before he trusts it with his depot network. Branches A, B and C.
  • Emma, a network scientist (persona), is working on a patent citation sample (124,318 patents, 1,480,221 citations), too big to draw, on a laptop with WebGPU. She works from the keyboard. Branch D.
  • Sarah, a fraud analyst (persona), has March's card and transfer data (3,000 accounts, 9,113 transfers) and a 14-account mule ring. Branch E.

AThe quiet trap: a weight read backwards Right-looking wrong answer

In Les Miserables the edge column value counts the scenes two characters share, so a higher number means a closer tie. Betweenness needs lengths. If the counts are read as lengths, the strongest ties become the longest paths, and the ranking that comes out looks reasonable.

A1The load step shows value as data only

Alex, operations analyst, the load step over a blank project.

He drops miserables.json on a blank project. The load step shows the edge column value as data only: whole numbers, 1 to 31, most edges 1 to 3. It says nothing about what a higher value means, because that is not a property of the column: each run that reads value asks it. The project keeps its blank name until Load commits.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Whole numbers on the edges. Fine."

Then: the graph loads as Les Miserables.

Open the full screen

A2The run asks what a higher value means

Alex, the Catalog in Results and Betweenness's run form.

Results is open on the rail. He clicks Betweenness in its Catalog. The run form reads the weight column value and asks "For value, a higher number means..." as four radio buttons with nothing chosen; Enter and Run do nothing until he answers. The graph's Statistics describe value only by its data: "value, shared scenes, 1 to 31".

Then: he reads the four answers.

Open the full screen

A3Four answers, each naming its conversion

Alex, Betweenness's run form.

Each answer carries one line saying how the run will turn value into a length: a closer or stronger link, Distance = 1 / value; a longer or costlier step, Distance = value. More can pass through and Don't use value are there too, in the same order as everywhere the question is asked. Nothing is picked for him. He thinks of a number on an edge as a length and picks a longer or costlier step; Run turns on.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"A number on an edge. Distance, I suppose."

Then: he presses Run.

Open the full screen

A4A plausible ranking, and no error

Alex, the run's row in Results, and the table.

Betweenness finishes at once and nothing warns. Valjean first, then Gavroche, Javert, Myriel, Thenardier; Marius 10th. Its row in Results names the run and the conversion it used: "Run 1. Distance = value". The row has no fill, because its record is not open.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Gavroche second, Javert third. Sounds about right."

Then: the design bets he stops at the conversion on the row. If he reads past it, see the miss path below.

Open the full screen

A5He changes the answer; Run 1 goes Out of date at once

Alex, Run 1's record, opened from its row in Results.

He opens Run 1 from its row. Its record shows the same question with his answer, and the top nodes it produced, headed "Run 1 (Distance = value)". He changes the answer to a closer or stronger link. This run's option changed, so Run 1 is Out of date at once, on its row and in the table's column header, with one verb, Re-run (keeps Run 1). Nothing reruns by itself: the old numbers stay, marked, until he asks. Nothing on the column changed, and no other result is touched.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"So that one's stale now."

Then: he presses Re-run (keeps Run 1).

Open the full screen

A6The ranking the data supports

Alex, the runs in Results, and the table.

Valjean 0.795, Marius 0.499, Myriel 0.224, Fantine 0.193, Courfeyrac 0.177. Marius moved from 10th to 2nd, Javert from 3rd to 45th. In Results, Run 2's row names the new conversion, "Distance = 1 / value", and Run 1 stays under it with its own, so both rankings can still be read.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Marius second. OK."

Open the full screen

Outcome. The wrong number never looked wrong. What can catch it is the question each weighted run asks, with nothing chosen for him, and the conversion the run names on its row in Results. The fix is made on the run: Run 1 goes Out of date the moment its answer changes, and Re-run keeps it beside Run 2.

The bet the study tests. The run's question prevents the mistake for most analysts, and for those who answer it wrong, the conversion on the run's row (A4) is noticed before a number is quoted.

Pass. Before quoting a ranking, the participant says which conversion the run used, or changes the answer in the run's record and re-runs.

Fail, the miss path. Alex reads past "Distance = value" on the row in A4, never opens the run, and pastes Javert as the third most central character into his deck. Seen in sessions, that means the conversion on the row is not doing its job.

BThe variant trap: closeness on a graph in pieces Right-looking wrong answer

Alex filters out Valjean, and Les Miserables falls apart into 7 components. Plain closeness then rewards a node for being close to the few others it can reach. graphty uses the Wasserman-Faust correction, which scales each score by how much of the graph the node can reach, and says so in the name.

B1Closeness names its formula before it runs

Alex, the Catalog in Results, Les Miserables with Valjean filtered out.

Without Valjean the graph falls into 7 components: the bishop's household of 10 is cut off from everyone, and 5 characters are left alone. He points at Closeness in the Catalog. The row already carries the word WF-corrected, and its tooltip says why: 7 components, each score scaled by the share of the graph the node can reach.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"WF? No idea what that is."

Then: he runs it.

Open the full screen

B2The result's name carries the variant

Alex, the run's row in Results, and the table.

The run's row in Results and the table's column are both named Closeness (WF-corrected): Javert 0.997, Enjolras 0.983, Courfeyrac 0.960, Marius 0.930, Combeferre 0.928. The bishop's household sits low; Myriel is 62nd. Clicking the variant words offers the one alternative that needs no correction, Harmonic centrality, as a new run beside this one.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Javert first. And what's Harmonic?"

Open the full screen

What the same run says without the correction

Not a graphty screen: this is closeness averaged only over the nodes each character can reach, as many tools compute it by default. The bishop's cut-off household takes two of the top five places, Myriel first, because its members are close to each other and to no one else. That ranking is the trap; the variant word in the name is what tells a reader which of the two a number came from.

#Closeness (WF-corrected), in graphtyvalueWithout the correctionvalue
1Javert0.997Myriel1.338
2Enjolras0.983Javert1.247
3Courfeyrac0.960Enjolras1.229
4Marius0.930Mme.Magloire1.205
5Combeferre0.928Courfeyrac1.200

Values near and above 1 are expected: lengths are 1 / value, under 1 for every tie of 2 or more shared scenes. Computed with NetworkX by failure-and-recovery-numbers.py.

Outcome. graphty never runs the misleading form silently: the correction is chosen for a graph in pieces, named before the run on the Catalog row, and carried in the run's name and the column header, so a number copied into a deck carries its formula.

The bet the study tests. An analyst who meets an unfamiliar variant word asks what it means (the tooltip, the (i)) before comparing the numbers with another tool's closeness.

Pass. Asked why Myriel is 62nd here but first in another tool's output, the participant points at the variant word, or opens its tooltip, and explains the difference in their own words.

Fail, the miss path. The word reads as noise. The participant compares graphty's Javert first with another tool's Myriel first and decides one of them is broken. The probe: ask what "WF-corrected" means to them before showing the tooltip. If most Alex-type participants cannot say, the word needs plainer wording (a two-way door, for the owner).

CThe wrong middle step, and three ways back Wrong-looking answer

Alex wants to know who holds the story together without its two protagonists. He built three filter steps, then re-ran betweenness. With Valjean gone, the bishop's household is its own island, and Filter to Largest component took all of it.

C1Fewer characters than expected

Alex, the filter chip and the table.

He wanted to know who holds the story together without Valjean and Javert: Filter out label = Valjean, Filter to Largest component (meant to drop the five characters left alone once Valjean was gone), Filter out label = Javert, then Re-run betweenness. The chip reads 60 of 77 nodes, 3 steps. Betweenness puts Marius first and Mme.Thenardier second at 0.467, and Myriel is nowhere.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Sixty? I took out two people."

Then: he opens the chip.

Open the full screen

C2The steps say where the 15 went

Alex, the filter steps.

Each step shows the number of nodes left after it: 76, 61, 60. The drop from 76 to 61 is the middle step. Pointing at it says so in words: 61 left. Took out 15: Myriel, Mlle.Baptistine, Mme.Magloire, Champtercier, Count and 10 more. With Valjean gone, the bishop's household was its own island.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Seventy-six to sixty-one. The bishop's lot."

Then: he looks for a way to take back just that step.

Open the full screen

C3Undo walks back from the newest change

Alex, the Edit menu.

Undo reads Undo Re-run betweenness, not the step he wants. Three presses, each labeled, would reach Filter to Largest component, and would take Filter out label = Javert and the run with them. Undo history, a temporary list that goes away once graphty-element can restore a canceled run on Redo, shows the same order; nothing in this branch needs it.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Undo goes the wrong way for this."

Then: he closes the menu and goes back to the steps.

Open the full screen

C4Way back one: turn the step off

Alex, the filter steps and the run's row in Results.

He clears the step's checkbox. It stays in the list with -- for its count; the step below recounts and the chip reads 75 of 77 nodes, 2 of 3 steps, at once. Betweenness still describes the old scope, so its row in Results reads "on 60 of 77" with Re-run. That is scope, not staleness, so its row carries no mark.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Off. Seventy-five."

Then: one undo step, Turn off step Filter to Largest component.

Open the full screen

C5Way back two: delete the step

The same moment, the other way: Alex, the filter steps.

With the step's row focused he presses Delete. It goes at once, with no question; the list closes up to two steps, focus moves to the next row, and the chip reads 75 of 77 nodes, 2 steps. Everything happened in sight, so there is no notice. The small inset is Edit afterwards: Undo Delete step Filter to Largest component, so this way back has its own way back.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Gone. Seventy-five."

Open the full screen

C6Re-run on the graph he meant

Alex, the table.

Re-run on 75 characters: Marius 0.307, Mme.Thenardier 0.296, Fantine 0.251, Cosette 0.247. The same order, every value lower.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Same order, smaller numbers."

Open the full screen

Outcome. Three ways back, each with a different cost: turning the step off (one click, keeps it), deleting it (one key, undoable), and undo (walks back from the newest change, so it also takes the good step after it and the run). The chip's count gave the mistake away; the per-step counts said which step.

The bet the study tests. An analyst who sees an unexpected count opens the chip, finds the step by its count, and turns it off or deletes it, rather than undoing.

Pass. Within the session task, the participant names the step that removed 15 characters and removes its effect without losing Filter out label = Javert.

Fail, the miss path. The participant presses Undo until the count looks right, losing Filter out label = Javert and the run, then rebuilds them; or never opens the chip and quotes the 60-node numbers.

DThe GPU is lost, and a run becomes costly No answer

Past the drawing limit nothing is drawn, so Results on the rail, the inspector and the table carry the work. graphty never finishes a GPU run on the CPU without saying so. Losing the GPU also changes what everything else costs: every later run goes to the CPU, which is why exact betweenness is refused at hours two frames later.

D1A re-run on WebGPU, the old values still shown

Emma, network scientist, the run's record in Results.

She changed damping from 0.85 to 0.5 and pressed Re-run. The run's record is open in place in Results, named PageRank, damping 0.5: 62%, the engine, WebGPU, and Cancel as its one verb. It says whose values are on screen until the new ones land: "Showing Run 1 (damping 0.85) until this run finishes." The running notice over the canvas repeats the run.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Let it cook."

Then: her laptop's graphics driver resets.

Open the full screen

D2The GPU is lost: a failed run, never a quiet CPU finish

Emma, the run's record in Results.

The run fails. Its record gives the cause, "Could not run PageRank: WebGPU lost; new runs use the CPU", and says whose values are on screen: "Showing Run 1 (damping 0.85). Run 2 wrote nothing." Two verbs follow. Re-run on CPU names where the next run goes; its tooltip gives the cost, a few minutes on the CPU. Try WebGPU again asks graphty-element to reach the GPU again: an explicit retry the element owns, not a fallback, and it re-runs nothing by itself. The raw code is the last line of Details.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Driver reset. So this is 0.85 still."

Then: she goes back to the list before deciding.

Open the full screen

D2BBack in the list, the row alone says whose values are shown

Emma, Results.

The failed run's row keeps its cause, Failed: WebGPU lost, and the same line, "Showing Run 1 (damping 0.85). Run 2 wrote nothing.", with Re-run on CPU and Try WebGPU again on the row, so the list answers the question without opening anything. Run 1, damping 0.85, is the row under it.

Then: she presses Re-run on CPU. Had Try WebGPU again reached the GPU, the graph's Statistics would read Engine: WebGPU and the next run would use it.

Open the full screen

D3A costly run is refused before it starts

Emma, the record of Betweenness in Results.

PageRank has re-run on the CPU as Run 3. She asks for Betweenness. With WebGPU lost every run goes to the CPU, where the element estimates exact betweenness at hours, past the 30-second time limit. It is not started: its record opens in place, reads "Not run: would take hours. The time limit is 30 seconds.", and lists the ways forward, cheapest first. Fits the time limit: Sampled, 101 sources, under a minute; Exact, on the 5,318 nodes in Drug patents granted in 2001, under a minute, marked "This is a different graph." Past the time limit: Exact, on the full graph, hours. Sampled is the default: it is first and focused, the one verb reads Run sampled, and Enter runs it. Try WebGPU again sits beside the cause, because the GPU is what made it hours.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Sampled is fine for a first look."

Then: she presses Enter.

Open the full screen

D4The sampled run starts; she cancels it from the notice

Emma, Results and the running notice.

Enter ran the default. Betweenness (sampled) runs at once on the CPU, 101 sources, 18%, as a new row at the top of Results; the refused Betweenness stays under it, "Not run: would take hours." Her own baseline for this graph used 500 sources, and the refusal offered only the default sample size. She presses Cancel on the running notice.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"101 sources. My baseline is 500."

Open the full screen

D5Canceled: nothing kept, focus on the row

Emma, Results, keyboard in hand.

The notice is gone and nothing of the canceled run is kept. It was the run's first attempt, so the row reads Not run, with Run, as a result created unrun does. Keyboard focus is on the row, with its ring visible, not lost to the page, so Enter opens its record. (The page also announces "Betweenness (sampled) canceled. Run".)

Then: she presses Enter.

Open the full screen

D6Set the sample, and run

Emma, the record of Betweenness (sampled) in Results.

Enter opens the run's record in place. She tabs to Sample size and types 500. Under the field: about 101 fits the time limit; 500 takes a few minutes and runs in the background. Run starts it.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"A few minutes is fine. Go."

Open the full screen

Outcome. Nothing ran on a path Emma did not see named first. The lost GPU showed as one failed run with its cause, the old values kept and named ("Showing Run 1 (damping 0.85). Run 2 wrote nothing."), a button that says where the next run goes, and Try WebGPU again, a retry graphty-element performs only when asked. The costly run was refused before it started with the ways forward listed, the default was the cheap one, and the cancel left nothing behind and put focus where she could act.

The bet the study tests. After a failure the analyst can say whose values are on screen; at a refusal she chooses a route knowing its cost.

Pass. Asked after D2 or D2B which damping the shown PageRank used, the participant says 0.85. At D3 she can say, before choosing, what each route costs.

Fail, the miss path. She reads the D2 numbers as the 0.5 run and reports them; or at D3 presses Enter without reading and later quotes the sampled scores as exact. The row's (sampled) name and the scores' estimate marks are the net for the second.

ESelecting everything Wrong-looking answer

graphty-element marks up to 5,000 selected elements one by one. Past that it keeps every id but draws the selection as one outline with a count, because thousands of rings would hide the drawing they sit on. Selecting is not an undo step, so the undo chord does something else.

E1Fourteen accounts, each with its own ring

Sarah, fraud analyst, the canvas and the Sets list.

The 14 flagged accounts are selected, each with its ring, and she has just kept them as the set Mule ring.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Now the whole list, for the case file."

Open the full screen

E2Select all: one hull and a count

Sarah, the canvas.

Out of spreadsheet habit she presses Ctrl+A. 3,000 accounts and 9,113 transfers are selected, 12,113 elements, past the cap of 5,000. The canvas draws one outline in the selection colors with the count; the inspector and table take over.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Oops. That's everything."

Open the full screen

E3The reflex: Ctrl+Z deletes the set

Sarah, the Sets list.

She presses Ctrl+Z to get her fourteen back. Selecting is not an undo step, so Undo reverses her last command, Create set Mule ring: the set's row disappears from Sets and paths, and everything is still selected. The row was in sight, so there is no notice.

Expected reaction (a hypothesis, not a finding)

"Still everything. Where's my set?"

Open the full screen

E4Redo brings the set back

Sarah, the Edit menu.

She opens Edit. Redo names what it restores: Redo Create set Mule ring.

Then: she chooses Redo; the set's row is back.

Open the full screen

E5Select members on the set, not undo, brings back the 14

Sarah, the Edit menu.

Undo reads Undo Create set Mule ring again. Select members on the Mule ring row selects the 14 accounts. Ctrl+Z would not: it brings back only a selection that Esc or a click on empty canvas cleared, and Select all replaced the 14.

Then: the 14 are selected again, as in E1.

Open the full screen and the 14 selected (E1)

Outcome. The drawing stayed readable and the count stayed exact. The reflex, Ctrl+Z, removed the set she had just made, and Redo brought it back; Select members on the set restored the fourteen without undoing work. Today graphty-element truncates a selection past the cap instead of holding every id; this design needs that changed in the element.

The bet the study tests. Frames E4 and E5 are the hoped-for path. The study records whether analysts reach for the undo chord first.

Pass. The participant gets the 14 back with the Mule ring set intact, by selecting the set's members.

Fail, the miss path. She presses Ctrl+Z (E3) and does not see the set's row go, because her eyes are on the canvas and no notice appears; she carries on without the set. If one participant in five misses the lost set, the in-sight rule for undo notices needs a second look for sets.

What this storyboard decides

Where the design documents were silent or unclear, these frames make a choice. Each is proposed in framework-changes.md with its evidence, and none is final until the study tests it.

  • Runs have one home, Results on the rail: every run of a measure, with its settings and date. Opening a run shows its record in place. Values are still read on the node, in the inspector and in the table.
  • Each weighted run asks what a higher value means, with nothing chosen, and Run stays disabled until it is answered (A2, A3). The column describes only its data.
  • A weighted run names the conversion it used on its row in Results (A4, A6).
  • In Statistics, the weight has its own row, Weight, beside Edges and Direction, so two rows are not both labeled Edges.
  • A run's row takes the selected fill only while its record is open (A4, A5).
  • Each filter step shows the count left after it, and pointing at a step names whom it took out (C2), as the filter-chip work already proposes.
  • While a run's record is open its verbs are in the record, and once it is closed they are on the run's row (D1, D2, D2B).
  • A running or failed run says whose values are on screen: "Showing Run 1 (damping 0.85) until this run finishes" while it runs, and "Showing Run 1 (damping 0.85). Run 2 wrote nothing." once it has failed, in its record and on its row (D1, D2, D2B).
  • A run that failed because WebGPU was lost offers Try WebGPU again: an explicit retry that graphty-element performs, not a fallback, and it re-runs nothing by itself (D2, D2B, D3).
  • The over-budget refusal lists the routes cheapest first, grouped by whether they fit the time limit, with the first focused and named on the one button: the sampled method is the default (D3), as already proposed for the run-and-read work.
  • Canceling from the running notice puts keyboard focus on the result's row (D5), as already proposed for the run-and-read work.

Screens

  • The quiet trap: a weight read the wrong way: six states.
  • The variant trap: closeness on a graph in pieces: two states.
  • The wrong middle step: three ways back: seven states.
  • When the GPU is lost, and when a costly run is canceled: seven states.
  • A selection past the cap: five states.

Every screen has a light and dark switch and an annotation layer naming the design section and the compact-mantine component behind each element. Numbers come from the kit's fixtures; the weighted and filtered runs were computed from the same Les Miserables file by failure-and-recovery-numbers.py.
